text:
Lynelle Johnson, director of child nutrition and food distribution for the Department of Public Instruction, speaks to Legislative Management during a hearing on a free school meals ballot measure on June 11, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota lawmakers this week adopted an official cost estimate for a free school meals ballot measure that voters will consider in November.
The Department of Public Instruction estimates the cost to implement the free school meals ballot measure would range between $124.3 million to $134.3 million every two years.
The cost range for providing free breakfast and lunch to public K-12 students is slightly lower than estimates presented to lawmakers in December. Officials revised the estimate after talking with nine other states that established similar programs, Lynelle Johnson, director of child nutrition and food distribution for the Department of Public Instruction, told lawmakers.
Free school meals measure in North Dakota approved for November vote

Legislative Management, a committee with members from the House and Senate, on Thursday voted to use the new estimate as the fiscal estimate for Measure 3 that will appear on the general election ballot. The cost analysis will be found next to the ballot measure language on the Secretary of State’s website.
Johnson said the new estimate is based on participation in federally subsidized free and reduced-cost school meal programs in other states that offer free school meals. She said more schools are expected to use other reimbursement programs, like SNAP, the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program and Medicaid, for income verification to automatically qualify for the federal school meals program.
“Over the past two years we’ve used cautious assumptions because we really weren’t sure how many families would still fill out applications,” Johnson said.
An application to receive free or reduced school meals requires families to provide household income data to establish how much of the meal cost would be reimbursed through the federal or state government.
In North Dakota, about 125,000 students attend schools that participate in the federal school lunch program, Johnson said. She added there are only a few thousand students that attend smaller public schools, private schools, or are homeschooled, that don’t participate in the program.
Johnson said North Dakota could follow Vermont’s model for universal school meals. In that state, schools are required to participate in other reimbursement programs, which automatically enroll students at the federal level for school meals programs. The automatic enrollment could reduce the reliance on annual income verification applications that parents submit to schools, she said.
Sen. Janne Myrdal, R-Edinburg, a member of Legislative Management, said she worries that people aren’t going to continue to apply for the free or reduced meals program and the cost of providing the meals will balloon because the state won’t receive as much federal funding.
“I think the general public out there is going to go, ‘Free is free,’ so I fear that we’re going to hit $150 million to $170 million pretty quickly in the next couple of bienniums,” Myrdal said.
Ballot measure effort seeks to provide free school meals to North Dakota students

Rep. LaurieBeth Hager, D-Fargo, said she realizes the price tag on the program is large, but said feeding about 125,000 students a meal for about 175 days per year is an investment.
The Secretary of State’s Office approved and verified more than 49,000 petition signatures to get Measure 3 on the ballot.
If approved by voters, the free school meals program will take effect for the 2027-28 school year. Private and tribal colleges would be able to opt in to the program.
The measure specifies that the state’s Legacy Fund would be used to pay for the free breakfasts and lunches unless the Legislature identifies other funding.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Michael Achterling can be reached at machterling@northdakotamonitor.com.

text:
Should School Revenue Process Allow “Automatic Increases” or Referendums for Even Modest Inflation Impacts?
DOVER — Delaware senators advanced a school-finance bill Thursday that supporters say would prevent large post-reassessment tax surprises while giving districts a steadier way to keep up with rising costs, but critics warn the proposal would weaken voter control over property-tax increases.
Senate Bill 322 would repeal a decades-old provision that allows school districts to raise operating revenue by up to 10% after a general reassessment. In its place, the bill would limit post-reassessment collections to prior operating revenue plus a factor tied to taxable property growth, and would allow most school districts to increase referendum-approved operating taxes by up to 2% annually without a new referendum if their operational reserves do not exceed 10% of annual revenue.
Senate President Pro Tempore, David Sokola (SD8)
The measure, sponsored by Senate President Pro Tempore Dave Sokola and House Speaker Melissa Minor-Brown, follows public frustration after Delaware’s first broad property reassessments in decades. Some homeowners saw higher tax bills, driven in part by shifts in the tax burden and, in several districts, use of the existing 10% authority.
Speaker, Melissa Minor-Brown (Dem – RD17)
The proposal is also part of a longer-running debate over how Delaware pays for public schools. Under current law, districts generally must ask voters in a referendum before increasing operating tax rates, even when the request is meant to cover routine cost pressures such as salaries, utilities, transportation, classroom supplies, maintenance and student services. Supporters of SB 322 say that structure can force districts to delay modest inflationary adjustments until they need a larger referendum, creating financial uncertainty for schools and more abrupt choices for taxpayers.
That concern grew as districts across the state faced higher costs and, in some cases, returned to voters after years without operating increases. Backers argue the bill’s limited 2% annual authority would not replace referenda, but would give eligible districts a narrow tool to maintain services approved by voters while absorbing part of the normal rise in costs between referenda.
Supporters argue the bill is a more measured alternative to sudden reassessment-related increases and a response to a funding system that can require districts to seek voter approval for relatively small operating adjustments. “This legislation eliminates the 10% post-reassessment increase and replaces it with a more predictable, transparent approach,” Sokola said. He has argued Delaware’s current referendum-centered system can leave districts unable to respond to inflation, enrollment changes and student needs, particularly in communities with less property wealth. Minor-Brown said the bill is intended to bring “fairness, transparency and predictability” to taxpayers while preserving school resources.
Under the bill, the new reassessment formula would take effect after the next general reassessment. Districts could not begin using the annual 2% authority until after that reassessment or fiscal year 2031, whichever comes first. The proposal also would not allow districts to raise taxes by more than 2% without voter approval, and capital projects would continue to require referenda.
Opponents, including the Caesar Rodney Institute’s Center for Economic and Fiscal Policy, say the annual 2% authority would put school property taxes on “autopilot.” “SB 322 would allow school districts to raise operating taxes year after year without asking voters,” the group argued in its analysis. Critics say even a modest yearly increase compounds over time and could burden homeowners, seniors on fixed incomes, small businesses and landlords already facing other rising costs.
Critics also question whether the bill’s reserve limitation is clear enough, noting that “operational reserve balance” and “annual revenue” could require further definition. “Before granting automatic taxing authority, lawmakers should require districts to show stronger fiscal discipline and academic results,” the institute said. Opponents also argue that districts should demonstrate efficiency before receiving any automatic taxing authority, especially in districts where enrollment has declined.
Supporters counter that the current 10% reassessment mechanism is blunt and unpredictable, while the proposed annual limit is smaller, delayed and subject to financial guardrails. “This is about avoiding sudden spikes while giving schools a responsible way to plan,” supporters of the measure have said. They say the bill would help districts maintain existing services and cover modest inflationary increases without waiting for large referendum requests that can fail after costs have already increased.
The debate reflects a broader tension in Delaware school funding: how to balance local taxpayer approval with the need for stable revenue in a system affected by reassessment, inflation, student needs and uneven enrollment trends across districts.
SB 322 now awaits consideration in the House of Representatives.
